posts.name: Chief Lackey Rich
posts.cooked:
As a distributor, FRG is also caught in a foreseeable Malachi Crunch if the tariff situation continues for any real period of time. The industry is probably headed for a massive contraction as publishers collapse or scale back to direct sales only, which will starve the distribution network, which in turn will lead to retail stores failing - especially if sales overall drop along with discretionary income as the rest of economy stutters. If that pattern goes on for long, even if things turn around who’s a distributor supposed to sell to? A few surviving stores, most of which will have gotten used to ordering direct from publishers? And how much will even be available to sell with many publishers gone for good?

I’ve worked through the sports card and comic book boom-and-bust cycles. Those were mild blips mostly caused by speculators and publisher overproduction compared to this idiotic trade war, and they still killed half the specialist shops that existed before the booms started. I’ll be amazed if one game store in five survives this mess, and one in ten might be more realistic unless it ends tomorrow.

posts.name: MindWanderer
posts.cooked:
The RPG getting suspended makes sense to me—if it even is. Most of the work that’s holding it up is either done by contracted writers (who can’t be “let go” as they’re not employees) or by Christopher. Not a lot of it seems to be actively being worked on by other full-time employees.

But also, the RPG isn’t making money. RPGs have razor-thin margins at best, due to the amount of work that goes into them, the price of books, and the diminishing returns you get on successive expansions on the same product. How much more investment would be needed to actually put out a product at this point? And what would the sales be? It was one thing to have people working on it in addition to other things, as a passion project, but from a corporate overlord perspective I can see why it wouldn’t make sense to continue.

And the podcast… that’s a good question. Trevor certainly could be paid as a freelancer, as he used to be, and as he certainly still is for Ludological Alchemy. The Patreon brings in enough money to pay him. But it likely doesn’t make much profit, if any, beyond breaking even. FRG may simply not want to be bothered. Especially since the podcast is effectively an investment in future content that FRG may be thinking they don’t want to make.

That wasn’t quite what happened. The guy/small business that created the original project overpromised on stretch goals, couldn’t handle them all, and wound up having a heart attacke that closed his business and saw him leave gaming altogether. A friend of his with a similar business agreed to step in and try to fulfill the project (in exchange for the rights to the figures and molds that had been done, which he hoped to sell at retail after the KS was finished. That led to partial fulfillment, but he overreached as well and wound having to admit he’d never finish everything, so another guy came along, picked up the rights, and did his best to continue fulfillment. That was the stage where i got everything I’d backed for, plus another pledge that someone sold me, plus some extras that I agreed to pay for to help Guy #3 pay postage on my stuff and some other pledges (by that point I figured we’d never see retail sales, so I wanted everything I’d ever need while I could get it). I only got everything because I was a merciless pest about it to three different people, and because i was willing to throw some actual outside-of-KS-funds money to speed the process up. I think there may be a fourth business involved now but I haven’t really paid attention. Last I was involved about 2/3rds of the backers had their stuff, and AFAIK none of them paid multiple times for their pledges - but I know a few did what i did and agreed to order some extra figs at retail to keep the engine sputtering along.

Convoluted as it sounds, it actually wasn’t the worst kickfailure I’ve been involved with, but it was the last of them. No more crowdfunding for me, no matter what.

Still haven’t painted all of the minis, but the ones I have finished are pretty neat, so there’s that, anyway.

Sometimes they’re backers themselves who are determined to get their stuff or die trying, sometime they’re folks in the same industry/hobby niche who can afford to make things better and maybe hope to take over the ready-made audience for future sales someday, and sometimes they just feel bad for the backers and the creator and enjoy playing fulfillment angel for both of them.

Sadly, I think you have to get really lucky for something like that to happen. Usually a kickfail is just a kickfail and ends badly for most or all of the people who backed.
